routes.description: Establish that human freedom requires genuinely live alternatives and agent sourcehood, and that deliberative experience, constrained indeterminacy, executive selection, and cumulative self-formation can jointly supply those conditions despite biological and social limits.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if alternative-capable deliberation and agent contribution are necessary for freedom and responsibility, if indeterminism can operate through rather than replace rational selection, and if deterministic proximal agency cannot preserve the required authorship.

motionBridge.description: Show that freedom requires both genuinely available alternatives and an agent-originating contribution that deterministic practical agency cannot supply.

centralBridges.description: Establish that first-person deliberation and practical inquiry present alternatives as genuinely available rather than merely hypothetical.
Explain how constrained neural indeterminacy and executive criteria permit rational selection without reducing choice to either prior determination or randomness.
Show that agents originate action and progressively shape their own characters through repeated alternative-capable choices under inherited constraints.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that neuroscience does not decisively show conscious deliberation to be causally idle or choices to be settled before awareness.
Provide a non-dualist account on which conscious valition, brain-level realization, top-down constraint, and indeterminacy can belong to one agent.

routes.description: Establish that determinism preserves practically important freedom through willing action, consent, proximal causation, character, and responsibility practices, without requiring categorical alternatives or ultimate self-origination.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if meaningful distinctions between choices and nonchoices remain available under determinism, if persons can act through their brains and characters as proximal sources, and if libertarian alternatives or sourcehood add no necessary, workable condition for responsibility.

motionBridge.description: Show that freedom, will, and responsibility retain burden-satisfying practical content under determinism without libertarian alternatives or ultimate sourcehood.

centralBridges.description: Ground freedom in durable distinctions among willing, unwilling, consensual, coerced, chosen, and unchosen conduct.
Show that an embodied person can be the causally effective proximal source of conduct through deliberation and character even when prior conditions determine it.
Explain responsibility through plural, practice-shaped concepts of praise, blame, answerability, and reactive attitudes rather than one libertarian essence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether genetics, upbringing, and restricted evaluative criteria leave libertarian agents with the ultimate authorship their account requires.
Require a principled account of when an alternative is genuinely live and how that status explains responsibility across constrained cases.

sections.title: The Required Standard of Human Freedom
sections.rationale: Defines the motion-level dispute between libertarian alternatives and sourcehood on one side and compatibilist willing, choice, and practical agency on the other.

sections.title: Deliberation and Genuine Alternative Possibilities
sections.rationale: Tests whether first-person deliberation and practical inquiry support genuinely open options or can coexist with a determined future understood from a third-person perspective.

sections.title: Indeterminism, Randomness, and Agential Selection
sections.rationale: Addresses whether constrained stochastic variation plus executive criteria can produce rational libertarian choice, or whether probabilistic weighting still fails to confer authorship.

sections.title: Sourcehood, Character, and Formative Constraints
sections.rationale: Compares cumulative libertarian self-formation with compatibilist proximal causation while accounting for the roles of genetics, upbringing, evaluative criteria, and constrained opportunities.

sections.title: Responsibility and Practical Agency Under Determinism
sections.rationale: Examines whether consent, coercion, willing conduct, blame, praise, and reactive attitudes preserve freedom-relevant distinctions without categorical alternatives or ultimate sourcehood.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Compatibilism should identify the important notions of freedom and willing that survive determinism rather than claim to preserve the libertarian conception unchanged.
moves.attributionBasis: The host addresses Joe before the answer, and the speaker explicitly identifies the position as his compatibilist view.

response.rationale: Constructively defines the compatibilist route by seeking freedom-relevant notions that survive determinism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A clear motion-framing constructive move within its class.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposal distinguishes surviving notions from preserving libertarian freedom unchanged.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It advances a methodological proposal rather than claiming that the full route is already proven.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reframing is internally consistent and directly identifies the intended compatibilist task.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual proposal is intelligible, though this span does not yet demonstrate which notions survive.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly states the motion-level compatibilist completion standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is assessed in this framing move.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley says compatibilism should ask which important notions of freedom and will survive determinism or remain orthogonal to it.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Ordinary deliberation presents agents as considering genuine alternatives, selecting among them, and acting, which supports libertarian freedom absent a sufficient reason to reject that experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The host directly asks Nathan for his position, and the answer begins with an explicit declaration that he is a libertarian.

response.rationale: Constructively grounds genuine alternatives in ordinary first-person deliberative experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A strong constructive statement with a compressed evidential bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The experience claim is clear, but the scope of the inference from experience to reality remains partly open.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The absent-reason defeater qualifies the claim, but phenomenology alone only modestly supports metaphysical openness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is usable but leaves a material bridge from seeming alternatives to genuinely available alternatives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Common deliberative phenomenology supports the premise, but its metaphysical evidential force is substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central bridge concerning deliberative alternatives.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states positive experiential support without treating a developed alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins describes considering several options as serious things one can do or refrain from doing, followed by selection and action.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: On monism or physicalism, a person's brain states are parts of that person, so neural causation does not displace personal agency or establish that the person was not the source.
moves.attributionBasis: The same identified Joe turn continues, using explicit references to his position on determinism and to what follows from taking physicalism seriously.

components.text: Whether neural activity displaces the deliberating person as the source of action.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses a category mistake in contrasting the person with the person's brain under physicalism and states that neural causation therefore does not eliminate personal sourcehood.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly defeats the displacement inference, though it does not settle categorical alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly conditional on monism or physicalism and keeps neural and personal causation distinct.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stated physicalist condition, the non-displacement consequence is appropriately forceful.

charity.alternative: Neural precursors could show that conscious personal deliberation is causally idle even if the brain belongs to the person.
charity.decisiveQualification: Part-whole identity blocks simple displacement but does not by itself establish that conscious deliberation is causally efficacious.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The part-whole reasoning is strong, with only a bounded bridge from embodiment to the relevant kind of agency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conditional conceptual argument is well supported, though it does not independently establish physicalism or conscious efficacy.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports embodied proximal sourcehood under determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly defeats the crude person-versus-brain inference, with a bounded omission about conscious efficacy.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley cautions that under physicalism it is mistaken to say the brain acted instead of the person, because the brain is part of the person.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Even if willing is determined, morally important distinctions between willing and unwilling conduct, including consent, survive and provide substantive content for compatibilist freedom.
moves.attributionBasis: This remains within Joe's uninterrupted answer and explicitly develops what compatibilists should retain if determinism is assumed by stipulation.

response.rationale: Constructively identifies willing, unwillingness, and consent as morally important distinctions preserved under determinism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A clear constructive articulation of practical agency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently limits its claim to important distinctions that survive determinism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The existence and importance of the willing-consent distinction are well matched to the conceptual support offered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from persistent distinctions to substantive practical content is explicit and consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Consent and willing conduct are specific representative cases, with only a bounded gap to a complete theory of freedom.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central willing-practical-agency bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive move does not assess a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley argues that willing and consent remain important even if the will is determined and asks which distinctions survive determinism.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Libet-style readiness potentials do not establish that unconscious activity causes conscious decisions or actions, because readiness activity can be dissociated from both deciding and moving.
moves.attributionBasis: Nathan takes the floor by returning to the Libet experiment and later refers approvingly to the researcher and interpretation he had introduced in his earlier answer.

components.text: Whether readiness-potential evidence establishes a causal sequence that displaces conscious decision.

response.rationale: The reply identifies dissociation among readiness activity, conscious decision, and movement as defeating the inference that readiness activity causes both latter events.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies the disputed inference and gives its defeating evidential consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully limited to what Libet-style readiness evidence fails to establish.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Dissociation weakens the causal inference, though saying it cannot be causal compresses alternative causal models.

charity.alternative: Readiness activity may be one probabilistic contributor rather than a sufficient cause invariably followed by decision and movement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Observed dissociation defeats a simple sufficient-cause inference but not every contributory-cause model.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dissociation argument is relevant but leaves a material bridge from nonconstant association to absence of causal contribution.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It cites concrete dissociation and an averaging account, while compressing verification and rival causal explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary empirical-underdetermination bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply handles the simple causal reading well but omits the decisive contributory-causation qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins cites cases separating readiness potential from conscious decision and motor action and offers averaged brain noise as an alternative explanation.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Indeterminism need not be random or reasonless, because probabilistically constrained variation can be evaluated and selected through deliberative processes as part of libertarian agency.
moves.attributionBasis: The host poses the determined-or-random objection and Nathan answers in a sustained libertarian voice, repeatedly characterizing what a libertarian can consistently maintain.

components.text: Whether libertarian indeterminism must reduce agency to reasonless randomness.

response.rationale: The reply rejects the determined-or-random dichotomy by distinguishing unconstrained chaos from probabilistically constrained variation evaluated through deliberation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive randomness inference and supplies an alternative mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: Constrained variation is clear, but the exact scope and operation of agential selection remain partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that indeterminism need not be reasonless matches the mechanism sketched.

charity.alternative: Even weighted stochastic variation may leave which admissible outcome occurs attributable to chance rather than the agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Constraints and deliberative evaluation narrow outcomes but do not alone explain authorship of the final stochastic resolution.

logicalCoherence.rationale: It defeats a false dichotomy but leaves a material bridge from constrained evaluation to agent-authored final selection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Probability distributions provide a concrete model, though neural application and the selection warrant remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central indeterminate-selection requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply avoids caricaturing randomness but omits the strongest residual authorship problem.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins distinguishes reasonless chaos from variation within probability constraints and says deliberative processes can evaluate and select among outputs.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: A decision produced by weighted stochastic variation may remain no better than randomness for purposes of authorship when the agent's weighting criteria constrain the possible result.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly adopts an incompatibilist perspective hypothetically and develops objections to weighted stochastic choice.

components.text: Whether constrained stochastic weighting makes the resulting selection authored rather than random.

response.rationale: The reply directly contacts the authorship bridge by arguing that stochastic output may remain random in the relevant sense and that weighting criteria themselves constrain the result.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive premise but presents the objection more tentatively than a full diagnostic defeat.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is recoverable, but 'randomness in some sense' leaves the relevant authorship standard partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated acknowledgment that the point requires careful development matches the tentative support.

charity.alternative: The agent may be identical with the system that forms and applies the weighting criteria, making constrained selection genuinely agential.
charity.decisiveQualification: System identity can explain whose criteria operate without showing how a stochastic resolution becomes authored.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection identifies a material unresolved bridge but does not fully specify why weighted stochasticity is authorship-defeating.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It relies primarily on conceptual pressure and a hypothetical response rather than a defended comparison of models.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central indeterminate-selection bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes criterial constraint while retaining the decisive question about stochastic authorship.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley says weighted stochasticity may be no better than randomness for authorship and asks how criteria and weightings determine the possible results.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: When the self is identified with the brain's executive or valitional system, the agent participates in imposing the criteria that constrain and govern indeterminate choice.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly answers the preceding probabilistic objection by asking what the choosing self could be and locating it in executive brain function.

components.text: Whether criteria and constraints belong to the agent rather than operating independently of the self.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the self with the brain's valitional executive function, thereby contacting the ownership component of the stochastic-authorship objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers ownership of criteria but not how the final indeterminate outcome is selected.

precisionFindings.rationale: The system identity is recoverable, but 'self' and 'valitional executive function' are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposed identification is offered conditionally and with appropriate modesty.

charity.alternative: Identifying the agent with the criterial system establishes ownership of constraints but not authorship of whichever stochastic possibility occurs.
charity.decisiveQualification: A further selection relation is needed between agent-owned criteria and the particular undetermined result.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The identity reply is coherent but leaves a material inference from system ownership to libertarian authorship.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The physicalist identification is plausible but asserted with little functional or empirical defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports metaphysical integration while only indirectly advancing full sourcehood.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply contacts the stronger objection but omits its decisive residual-selection qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins proposes that the person may be the brain or its valitional executive function and thus participates in imposing the relevant constraints.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Genetics and upbringing heavily constrain an agent's evaluative criteria and place much of the possible choice space outside the agent's control, challenging claims of ultimate sourcehood.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly presents the other incompatibilist line and closes by asking Hawkins how his libertarian account responds to it.

components.text: Whether agent-owned criteria confer sourcehood when those criteria were heavily formed by genetics and upbringing.
Whether constrained possibilities supply meaningful authorship when the constraint space is largely outside the agent's control.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges ownership and ultimate sourcehood by tracing criteria and the accessible choice space to factors outside the agent's control.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts both the self-identification and constrained-selection components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to heavy influence and constraint rather than total external determination.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The substantial formative influence claimed is matched by familiar representative factors and explicit qualifications.

charity.alternative: Agents can later revise inherited criteria through repeated reflective choices and learning.
charity.decisiveQualification: Later revision may yield partial self-formation without supplying ultimate control over the initial criteria and opportunities enabling revision.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument consistently distinguishes agent-level operation from ultimate control over the criteria enabling it.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genetics and upbringing are specific representative constraints, with a bounded gap concerning their degree in individual cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central sourcehood and self-formation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection leaves room for later modification while preserving its qualified sourcehood challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley says evaluative criteria are heavily influenced by genetics and upbringing and that many possibilities are excluded by factors outside the agent's control.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Despite biological, social, and environmental limits, agents contribute through repeated choices and learning to reshaping their brains, expanding later options, and realizing themselves over time.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins expressly accepts limits on libertarian freedom and develops a positive account of constrained choice reshaping later character and possibilities.

components.text: Whether inherited constraints prevent agents from contributing to the formation of their later criteria and capacities.

response.rationale: The reply concedes biological and social limits but argues that repeated decisions and learning alter the brain, capacities, and later option set.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the possibility of later self-formation, though not the ultimate-source regress.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative and constrained character of self-realization is expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim of partial contribution rather than absolute self-creation fits the example and qualifications.

charity.alternative: Every apparently self-forming decision may itself express inherited criteria, so cumulative change need not provide ultimate authorship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cumulative plasticity demonstrates agent-involving formation but does not terminate the regress about the sources of earlier criteria.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative mechanism is coherent, with one bounded but important gap between participation and ultimate sourcehood.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Learning Greek concretely illustrates neuroplastic capacity expansion, though the libertarian causal contribution remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central self-formation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response addresses severe formation constraints but omits the decisive ultimate-source qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins argues that many small decisions reshape brain function over time, using learning Greek as an example of expanding later capacities and options.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: A libertarian model may not deliver the ultimate responsibility commonly expected of it when a restrictive environment prevents an agent from developing access to materially different evaluative criteria.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley states his concern about self-causing libertarianism and develops the racist-upbringing example as a challenge to Hawkins's restricted criteria account.

components.text: Whether cumulative self-formation provides expected libertarian responsibility when restrictive environments block alternative criteria.

response.rationale: The reply tests cumulative self-formation against a restrictive environment and argues that the resulting libertarian responsibility is more modest than commonly expected.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the scope of self-formation but does not show that the qualified account fails on its own terms.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clear, though 'ultimate responsibility commonly expected' has a partly unstable constituency and scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents the conclusion as a modest concern rather than a decisive disproof.

charity.alternative: A degree-based libertarian can accept reduced responsibility whenever social conditions restrict access to evaluative alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: That concession preserves coherence but yields less ultimate responsibility in precisely the restricted cases under discussion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The restricted-outlook case supports the qualified conclusion, with a bounded gap from modest responsibility to failure of libertarianism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The environmental case is relevant and concrete, though its generality and comparison with compatibilism are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary formation-constraints bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly recognizes that the opposing account may be modest while explaining the cost of that qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley considers an agent whose environment blocks different evaluative criteria and concludes that Hawkins's libertarian responsibility is substantially more modest than standard expectations.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Indeterminate neuronal firing can lack a sufficient determining cause while system-level criterial constraints exert top-down causation, providing a physical mechanism for agential selection.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins directly answers the demand for an uncaused neuron by describing synaptic indeterminacy and system-level criterial causation in the cited model.

components.text: Whether a physical mechanism can combine undetermined neuronal events with agent-level criterial control.
Whether system-level criteria can exert causal influence despite lower-level and formative constraints.

response.rationale: The reply supplies a top-down criterial-causation model in which system constraints govern neuron-level indeterminacy, contacting the mechanism demand more than the ultimate-formation demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a direct mechanism but leaves the authorship and criterion-formation objections partly unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The levels and causal roles are recoverable, but criterial or formational causation is only briefly defined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately presents a possible physical mechanism rather than an empirically established result.

charity.alternative: Top-down constraints may describe system organization without making the particular undetermined outcome agent-authored.
charity.decisiveQualification: Constraint of an outcome space is not yet a complete account of selection of one outcome within it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The multilevel mechanism is coherent in outline but leaves a material bridge from constraint to authorship of the particular result.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanism is largely theoretical in the span, with neural indeterminacy and top-down efficacy not independently substantiated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central indeterminate-selection mechanism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The mechanism addresses crude lower-level exclusion but omits the strongest selection qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins distinguishes lack of a sufficient neuron-level cause from system-level criterial constraints exerting top-down causation.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Freedom operates among alternatives genuinely live for an agent, while severe biological or social constraints can narrow those alternatives and correspondingly reduce moral responsibility by degree.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins distinguishes impossible or psychologically unavailable options from live alternatives and applies that distinction to responsibility for racist beliefs.

components.text: Whether restrictive formation eliminates responsibility or instead narrows live alternatives and responsibility by degree.
Whether biology and social formation constrain the alternatives actually attributable to an agent.

response.rationale: The reply preserves the formation concern but replaces an all-or-nothing demand with live options and degree responsibility, explaining that constraints reduce rather than invariably erase freedom.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It justifies and answers a replacement demand that retains the legitimate constraint issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: The degree claim and constraint scope are clear, but the threshold for a 'live option' remains only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The degree-theoretic conclusion is explicitly qualified by biological and social limitations.

charity.alternative: Without a principled test for liveness, degree responsibility may merely relabel intuitive judgments about constrained cases.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reframe is coherent but still owes a noncircular criterion for which options are genuinely live.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The degree reframe is coherent, with one important compressed bridge concerning the live-option criterion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Constraint examples support graded responsibility, but no independent method for identifying live options is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary demand that restrictive formation defeats the libertarian account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply handles the all-or-nothing alternative fairly but omits the decisive criterion problem.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins concedes that biological constraints affect freedom, requires alternatives to be live for the agent, and makes responsibility degree-theoretic.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: An alternatives-based account needs a principled way to determine when an option was genuinely live, particularly in cases where restrictive upbringing appears to exclude alternative evaluative paths.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn follows Nathan Hawkins's account of constrained live options and is framed in the first person as an incompatibilist challenge before discussing Jojo evidence.

components.text: What principled standard determines whether an alternative was genuinely live for a particular agent.
Whether restrictive upbringing permits access to materially different paths of self-formation.

response.rationale: The reply directly requests a criterion of liveness and tests the account against socioeconomic and restrictive-upbringing cases.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive missing criterion and a central application case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand is clear and tied to particular constrained cases rather than all alternatives generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A principled liveness criterion is necessary for the proposed responsibility distinctions to do explanatory work.

charity.alternative: Live options could be identified by the agent's reasons, capacities, and accessible evaluative outlook rather than metaphysical possibility alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those factors still require thresholds and a principled explanation of why excluded outlooks reduce responsibility to a particular degree.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The criterion demand follows directly from the degree-theoretic use of live options.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Restrictive upbringing and socioeconomic formation provide representative test cases, with only bounded generalization limits.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It very strongly supports the subsidiary live-option-criterion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge allows a contextual criterion while correctly preserving the need for principled thresholds.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley asks how an option becomes live for someone and compares the problem with arguments based on economic and restrictive upbringing.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Responsibility rests partly on an agent's alternative-capable role in gradually shaping the character from which later settled conduct proceeds, not only on isolated proximal choices.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies his position as libertarian, answers the Jojo example, and develops a first-person account of character formation and responsibility.

components.text: Why later settled conduct may be responsible despite limited proximal alternatives.
Whether responsibility can arise through an earlier role in shaping the kind of person one becomes.

response.rationale: The reply shifts attention from isolated proximal options to the agent's cumulative alternative-capable role in shaping later character, contacting both responsibility demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the source of later responsibility but does not supply the requested criterion for which earlier options were live.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes proximal action from longitudinal character formation and limits responsibility accordingly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that self-formation partly grounds responsibility is appropriately qualified.

charity.alternative: Earlier character-shaping choices may themselves arise from inherited character and restricted live options.
charity.decisiveQualification: Longitudinal relocation of responsibility does not by itself resolve the regress or establish liveness of earlier alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The longitudinal account is coherent but leaves a material bridge concerning responsibility for the earlier self-forming choices.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Human character formation is a plausible basis, though the alternative-capable causal contribution remains largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sourcehood-through-self-formation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply engages restricted agency but omits the decisive regress qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins distinguishes proximal control from the morally important role people play over time in shaping the persons and desires from which they later act.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Freedom and responsibility comprise plural, practice-shaped concepts whose content can be reconstructed through praise, blame, coercion, and reactive attitudes rather than one metaphysical formula.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley continues the same uninterrupted turn, surveys several compatibilist traditions, and explicitly advances a pragmatic reconstruction from responsibility practices.

components.text: How responsibility should be understood if no single metaphysical sourcehood formula captures all practices.
Whether responsibility can be reconstructed through graded practical attitudes rather than categorical alternatives.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing a single metaphysical essence with plural practice-shaped concepts grounded in praise, blame, coercion, and reactive attitudes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It preserves the responsibility issue and gives a substantive replacement framework, though its normative criteria remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The plural-practice thesis is clear, though the boundaries among the reconstructed concepts remain partly unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The exploratory pragmatic proposal is calibrated to its conceptual and practice-based support.

charity.alternative: Practices of praise and blame may themselves presuppose genuine sourcehood and alternatives rather than replace them.
charity.decisiveQualification: A pragmatic reconstruction must justify revising practices instead of merely reporting them, but their plurality still challenges a single essence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The pragmatic reframe is coherent, with one important compressed bridge from existing practices to justified reconstruction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several representative responsibility practices are identified, though no systematic comparison or normative test is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central responsibility-practices bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly opens a different explanatory route while leaving a bounded normative-justification omission.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley surveys praise, blame, coercion, and reactive attitudes and proposes pragmatically shaping these plural concepts rather than deriving them from one metaphysical formula.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Taking deliberative phenomenology and practical causal reasoning seriously supports treating agents as originating sources and their apparent ability to do otherwise as real rather than irrelevant.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker announces an attempt to persuade Joe toward libertarianism on Joe's pragmatic grounds and develops the argument using deliberation, causation, and responsibility.

components.text: Whether pragmatic attention to actual deliberation supports libertarian sourcehood rather than a purely compatibilist reconstruction.
Whether apparently originating agency and the ability to do otherwise should count among the important notions retained.

response.rationale: The reply turns Folley's pragmatic methodology toward first-person causal reasoning and alternative experience, arguing that these favor real sourcehood.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly engages the pragmatic frame, though the bridge from practical indispensability to metaphysical truth remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is recoverable, but 'taking phenomenology seriously' and 'uncaused cause' shift between practical and metaphysical senses.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Practical causal self-conception supports relevance but does not by itself make libertarian sourcehood probable.

charity.alternative: Compatibilists can treat deliberative phenomenology as practically indispensable while interpreting apparent openness counterfactually or epistemically.
charity.decisiveQualification: Pragmatic indispensability does not uniquely select a libertarian metaphysics without comparing the compatibilist interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument leaves a material bridge from first-person causal reasoning to uncaused sourcehood and categorical alternatives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Phenomenology is relevant evidence, but the metaphysical conclusion relies substantially on assertion and lacks rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion-level claim that compatibilist reconstruction is sufficient.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply contacts pragmatic compatibilism but omits its strongest nonlibertarian interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins says deliberators treat themselves as causes rather than as effects of prior chains and argues that serious attention to this phenomenology favors sourcehood.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: The evolved practical indispensability of conscious deliberation and inquiry supports taking their alternative-possibility structure seriously, including when interpreting the agency of other people.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins introduces two explicit further challenges, addresses Joe by name, and links evolutionary usefulness, inquiry, and interpersonal reactive attitudes to libertarian agency.

components.text: Whether pragmatic and evolutionary considerations support the alternative structure of conscious deliberation.
Whether conscious deliberation's practical role should be preserved as more than a merely hypothetical process.

response.rationale: The reply argues that the evolved usefulness of conscious deliberation and inquiry gives pragmatic reason to take their apparent alternative structure seriously.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It engages the pragmatic method directly but does not rule out deterministic usefulness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The deliberation and inquiry claim is clear, with an implicit qualification concerning what evolutionary usefulness establishes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Usefulness supports causal relevance more strongly than it supports genuinely open metaphysical alternatives.

charity.alternative: Deterministically realized conscious deliberation could be evolutionarily useful by processing reasons and modeling counterfactual options.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evolutionary usefulness does not distinguish categorical openness from useful deterministic counterfactual representation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A material bridge is missing from evolved usefulness and causal efficacy to libertarian alternative possibilities.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evolutionary premise is plausible, but its metaphysical interpretation is asserted without serious rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central deliberative-alternatives bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument does not adequately handle the strongest compatibilist explanation of usefulness.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins argues that conscious decision-making and inquiry were retained because useful, and infers that their alternative-possibility structure should be treated seriously.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Even if determinism were proven, distinctions between choices and nonchoices could remain intelligible, while tension between objective inquiry and first-person deliberation would burden theories of human inquiry generally.
moves.attributionBasis: Following Hawkins's request for the useful notion, Folley repeatedly identifies proximal sourcehood as his view and develops the object-versus-subject naturalism problem.

components.text: Whether useful deliberation and intelligible choice distinctions require an objectively open future.
Whether first-person agency becomes incoherent if objective inquiry supports determinism.

response.rationale: The reply denies the required inference by explaining that choices and nonchoices remain distinguishable under stipulated determinism and that the first-person/objective tension is a general problem for inquiry.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the necessity inference and states the surviving practical consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly conditional on determinism and distinguishes practical choice classifications from categorical openness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that distinctions could remain intelligible is fully matched to the stipulated thought experiment.

charity.alternative: Libertarians may accept verbal choice distinctions under determinism while denying that they preserve the freedom relevant to responsibility.
charity.decisiveQualification: Survival of a classification establishes practical content but not by itself the full normative adequacy of compatibilist freedom.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample coherently defeats the claim that intelligible choice distinctions logically require indeterminism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The deterministic stipulation and overwhelming-reason comparison support the conceptual possibility, with a bounded gap to moral sufficiency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central willing and choice distinction under determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly establishes the limited survival claim while leaving the stronger normative comparison open.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley says that even if determinism were proven beyond doubt he could still distinguish choices from nonchoices, including cases involving overwhelming reasons.
